references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the officer in Capernaum who comes to Jesus and asks for his servant to be healed. In Matthew, the officer comes himself, while in Luke he sends the elders among the Jews.
A royal official heard that Jesus had arrived and went to him to ask him to heal his son. A similar pattern where someone hears about Jesus and seeks his help to heal a sick person.
Jairus sends word and asks Jesus to come to heal his daughter, a similar pattern where someone asks Jesus to come to save someone who is dying.
Jesus went with them after being asked to come – a direct response to the request in verse 3 that Jesus should come and heal the servant.
Cornelius, another Gentile officer, sends men to bring Peter, in a similar way as the officer in Capernaum sent the Jewish elders to Jesus.
The synagogue leaders send word to Paul and Barnabas – an example of sending intermediaries with a request, just as the officer sent the elders.
Jesus sent messengers ahead, a similar pattern of sending others on his behalf to prepare for a meeting.
Naaman, the Syrian army commander, a Gentile of rank and power, seeks healing through God's prophet in Israel – a strong parallel to the Roman officer who seeks Jesus' healing power.
